title: Infancy Gospel of James

stories.title: 📜 Infancy Gospel of James
summaryBullets: Joachim, righteous yet childless, humbles himself through prayer and fasting, and Anna laments her barrenness (chapter 1).
An angel appears to Anna, announcing that she will conceive; Anna vows the child to the Lord’s service (chapter 2).
Joachim hears the promise as well, returns with abundant offerings, and Anna gives birth to a daughter named Mary (chapter 2).
As a child she grows strong; at age three, Joachim brings Mary to the Temple to fulfill her vow (chapter 7).
Mary is received by the high priest, placed on the temple steps, and anointed with divine favor (chapter 7).
She remains in the temple, receiving angelic food, and is cared for among the undefiled daughters of Israel (chapter 8).
When Mary reaches twelve, the priests seek a guardian for her (chapter 8).
All eligible widowers of Israel bring their rods to the altar for a sign from God (chapter 9).
Joseph’s rod miraculously blossoms, and a dove emerges, marking him as chosen (chapter 9).
Joseph, an older man, protests his unworthiness, but accepts guardianship of Mary (chapter 9).
The angel Gabriel appears to Mary, announcing she will conceive by the Holy Spirit (chapter 11).
Mary marvels at the message, asking how this can be, but submits to God’s will (chapter 11).
Joseph discovers her pregnancy and is troubled, fearing accusation (chapter 13).
An angel appears to Joseph in a dream, reassuring him that the child is of the Holy Spirit (chapter 14).
Joseph and Mary travel to Bethlehem for the census (chapter 17).
Mary is overtaken by labor, and they find a cave for shelter (chapter 18).
As Mary prepares to give birth, Joseph sees time miraculously stand still (chapter 18).
Mary gives birth in the cave, attended by a midwife (chapter 19).
A midwife named Salome doubts Mary’s virginity after childbirth (chapter 20).
When she tests Mary, her hand withers as punishment (chapter 20).
Salome cries out in pain, but is healed when she touches the infant Jesus (chapter 20).
The narrative closes with Mary’s purity confirmed and the child praised as the Savior.
crossRefs: Luke 1:5-25: Zechariah and Elizabeth are righteous and childless and both well on in years, and the angel meets him at the altar of incense with the promise of a son, the same pattern this book runs a generation earlier with Joachim and Anna.

Luke 1:26-38: Gabriel is sent to a virgin betrothed to a man named Joseph of the house of David, and she answers, Let it be to me according to your word, which is the annunciation this book retells in two stages, first at the well and then at her spinning.

Numbers 17:1-11: Twelve rods are laid up before the LORD overnight and Aaron's alone buds, blossoms and bears ripe almonds, settling which house holds the priesthood; this book runs the same test to decide which widower will take Mary.

Numbers 5:11-31: A wife suspected of unfaithfulness is brought to the priest and made to drink water mixed with dust from the tabernacle floor, and if she is innocent she is unharmed, which is the ordeal this book puts both Joseph and Mary through.
Matthew 1:18-25: Joseph finds Mary with child before they came together, decides to divorce her quietly, and is answered in a dream by an angel telling him the child is of the Holy Spirit.

Luke 2:1-7: Caesar Augustus orders a registration, Joseph goes up from Nazareth to Bethlehem with Mary who is expecting a child, and she wraps the newborn and lays him in a manger because there was no room in the lodging.

Exodus 26:31-33: The veil is woven of blue and purple and scarlet on fine twined linen with cherubim worked into it, the temple furnishing this book has Mary spinning thread for when the angel comes to her.

Matthew 13:55-56: The people of his own town name his brothers James, Joses, Simon and Judas and mention his sisters, the verse behind the reading this book takes for granted, that Joseph already had a household of his own when he took Mary.

translationNotes.note: Mary's parents are named here and nowhere in Scripture. Every later mention of Joachim and Anna, and every feast kept in their honour, traces back to this book. Anna is the same name as Hannah, and the opening chapters build her out of Hannah at 1 Samuel 1:9-18: childless, taunted for it, praying in bitterness of soul, and vowing the child to the Lord.

In a household that lived or died on its children, childlessness was a public disgrace and was spoken of that way. Genesis 30:23 has Rachel say at Joseph's birth that God has taken away her reproach, and Luke 1:25 has Elizabeth use the same word for the same relief. This book opens with Joachim turned away from bringing his offering because he has raised up no seed in Israel.

The book hands Mary over at three years old, sets her on the step of the altar, and has her raised inside the temple and fed by an angel. Nothing in the Law provides for that and no girl was reared in the temple. What the Law does require after a birth is at Leviticus 12:1-8, the purification and an offering, and Luke 2:22-24 has Joseph and Mary bring the pair of turtledoves that Leviticus allows in place of a lamb when the family is poor.

Choosing Joseph by a blossoming rod is Numbers 17:1-11 run a second time. There, twelve rods are laid before the LORD, one for each tribal house, and Aaron's alone buds, blossoms and bears ripe almonds overnight, settling the priesthood and ending the argument. This book adds a dove that comes out of the rod and settles on Joseph's head, which is the sign at the baptism in Matthew 3:16.

The priest makes Joseph and Mary each drink and sends them into the wilderness, and both come back unharmed. Numbers 5:11-31 is the law behind it: the suspected wife is brought to the priest, her offering is barley meal without oil or incense, and she drinks water mixed with dust from the tabernacle floor and with the words of the curse washed off the scroll into it. An innocent woman is cleared by it and bears children.

Betrothal in this period was legally binding and was not an engagement. The couple did not yet live together, but she was already called his wife and breaking it took a writ of divorce. Deuteronomy 22:23-24 puts a betrothed woman under the same law as a married one, which is why Matthew 1:19 can have Joseph plan to divorce a woman he has not yet married.

This book puts the birth in a cave beside the road, not in a stable and not in a house. Luke 2:7 says only that she laid him in a manger because there was no room in the kataluma, the guest room or lodging place. Justin Martyr, writing about AD 155 to 160 in the Dialogue with Trypho 78, also puts the birth in a cave near the village, so the tradition is at least that old.

Chapter 18 breaks into Joseph's own voice and has him look up to find everything halted: birds stopped in the air, workmen with their hands in the dish and not eating, sheep standing still under a shepherd's raised staff, and the sky itself at rest. Nothing of the kind appears in Matthew or Luke, which give the birth in a sentence and move straight on to the shepherds.

A woman named Salome refuses to believe the birth left Mary a virgin, tests her, and her hand is consumed as by fire until she touches the child. Clement of Alexandria refers to the examination in the Stromateis 7.16.93, which puts the episode in circulation by about AD 200. Luke 1:20 is the canonical shape of the same pattern, where Zechariah is struck dumb until the birth for asking how he could be sure.

A recognised trade, and one of the few a woman practised for pay. Exodus 1:15-21 names two of them, Shiphrah and Puah, who refuse Pharaoh's order to kill the Hebrew boys and are rewarded with households of their own. Genesis 35:17 has a midwife speak to Rachel as she dies bearing Benjamin. Here Joseph goes out to find one and comes back with her.

A registration for tax, taken household by household in the place a family was reckoned to belong. Luke 2:1-5 sends Joseph up from Nazareth to Bethlehem because he was of the house and lineage of David. This book has him stuck on how to enter Mary in the roll, since she is neither his wife nor his daughter, which is a question the Roman form would in fact raise.

Mary is one of the undefiled daughters of Israel given thread to spin for the temple veil, and the lot gives her the true purple and the scarlet. Exodus 26:31 lists those very colours for the veil, blue and purple and scarlet on fine twined linen. True purple came from the murex sea snail and took thousands of shells to dye a small piece of cloth, which is why purple marks out wealth and rank in passages like Mark 15:17 and Luke 16:19.

When the priest has to decide what is to be done with Mary he goes in to the altar and prays, and an angel answers him. The Law's provision for asking is at Exodus 28:29-30, the Urim and Thummim carried in the breastpiece of judgment over Aaron's heart. Numbers 27:21 has Joshua stand before Eleazar the priest, who inquires by the Urim, and the answer decides when Israel goes out and comes in.

The name now in common use is not ancient. Protevangelium means the gospel that stands before the Gospel, and it is the title Guillaume Postel gave his Latin translation, printed by Theodor Bibliander in 1552. The earliest witness is Papyrus Bodmer V, a Greek copy of the late third or early fourth century published by Michel Testuz in 1958, and about 140 Greek manuscripts survive.

This book makes Joseph an old man with sons already grown when he takes Mary, which is why he protests that he will be a laughing stock. Origen, in the tenth book of his Commentary on Matthew, reports that some held the brothers to be sons of Joseph by an earlier wife on the tradition of the Gospel of Peter or the Book of James. Matthew 13:55-56 names them and mentions sisters, and Galatians 1:19 calls James the Lord's brother.

translationNotes.term: The feasts built on this book
translationNotes.note: The Eastern churches keep three feasts whose whole content comes from this account rather than from Scripture: the Conception of Anna on 9 December, the Nativity of the Theotokos on 8 September, and the Entrance of the Theotokos into the Temple on 21 November. The hymns and the icons for those days follow this book scene by scene. The Latin West condemned the work by name in the Gelasian Decree.

stories.keyTakeaway: Twenty chapters covering the ground before Luke 1 and alongside Luke 2. Joachim and Anna are given a daughter after a vow, Mary is raised inside the temple, Joseph is chosen by a rod that blossoms, the birth happens in a cave with the whole world standing still around it, and a midwife named Salome tests Mary, loses the use of her hand, and is healed by touching the child.

intro:
The Infancy Gospel of James claims James for its author in its closing chapter, where the writer says he wrote the account in Jerusalem and withdrew into the wilderness when the death of Herod raised a tumult. The James claimed is James called the Lord's brother (Matthew 13:55, Galatians 1:19). The whole work runs twenty-five chapters. The text presented here runs from Joachim's offering to the healing of Salome, chapters 1 to 20.

The book covers the ground before Luke 1. Joachim, righteous and childless, and his wife Anna are named here as Mary's parents; Scripture does not name them, and every later mention of Joachim and Anna goes back to this book. An angel promises Anna a child and she vows the child to the Lord, as Hannah did (1 Samuel 1:11). Mary is born, brought to the temple at three, and raised there among the undefiled daughters of Israel. At twelve the priests gather the widowers of Israel with their rods, Joseph's rod blossoms and a dove comes out of it, and he takes her as his charge, protesting that he is old and has sons already. Gabriel comes to her (Luke 1:26-38). Joseph finds her with child, is troubled, and is answered in a dream (Matthew 1:20). They go up for the census (Luke 2:1-5), she is overtaken on the road, and the birth happens in a cave, with Joseph seeing the world stop still around him, a midwife called, and Salome doubting, testing, punished, and healed.

Papyrus Bodmer V is the earliest witness, a Greek copy of the late third or early fourth century, published by Michel Testuz in 1958. About 140 Greek manuscripts survive, along with Syriac, Coptic, Armenian, Georgian, Ethiopic, Arabic, Church Slavonic, and Latin versions. The name now in common use is not ancient. Protevangelium, the gospel that stands before the Gospel, is the title Guillaume Postel gave his Latin translation, printed by Theodor Bibliander in 1552.

The book was in circulation by about AD 200. Clement of Alexandria, in the Stromateis 7.16.93, reports that some say that after the birth Mary was examined and found to be a virgin, which is the Salome episode. Origen, in his Commentary on Matthew, book 10 section 17, writes that some hold, on the tradition of the Gospel of Peter or the Book of James, that the brothers of Jesus were sons of Joseph by an earlier wife.

The Latin West rejected it by name. The Gelasian Decree, transmitted under the name of Pope Gelasius I (AD 492-496) and dated in its present form to the sixth century, lists among the apocrypha the Gospel in the name of James the younger. The Eastern churches built on its account: the Conception of Anna on 9 December, the Nativity of the Theotokos on 8 September, and the Entrance of the Theotokos into the Temple on 21 November all rest on the events this book relates, and the hymnography and the iconography of those feasts follow it. No communion receives the book itself as canonical.
